html:
The golden rhinoceros of Mapungubwe is a small figure of a one-horned rhino, made of thin gold foil tacked onto a wooden core. It was found in 1932 in a royal grave on Mapungubwe Hill, in the far north of South Africa, and dates from the 13th century.

The kingdom of Mapungubwe grew up near where the Shashe meets the Limpopo. Its rulers lived on top of the hill, above their people, an early sign of a society split into rulers and commoners. They grew rich by sending gold and ivory down to the Swahili coast for Indian Ocean trade, and glass beads and cloth came back.

Mapungubwe faded in the 13th century, and power moved north to Great Zimbabwe. Under apartheid the finds were kept quiet, as they did not fit the claim that Africans had built no states. Today the rhino is held by the University of Pretoria, and South Africa's highest honour, the Order of Mapungubwe, is named after the kingdom.
